§9.5.5 Row-Label Hierarchy

📄 Page rule — applied from the page alone

tables-row-label-hierarchy · tables rule hierarchy encoding

✅ Normative

Where a table's row labels are indented to show nesting, every label cell MUST carry its absolute level as a data-level attribute: <td data-level="2">iPhone</td>. Level 0 is the leftmost label position in the stub column, 1 the next indent step, and so on — counted from the left edge of the column, never from the row above.

Financial statements and rate manuals encode hierarchy by indenting the row label. Flattened, "iPhone" and "Total net sales" read as siblings.

Printed stub:                     Rendered as:
Revenue                           <td data-level="0">Revenue</td>
  Products                        <td data-level="1">Products</td>
    iPhone          205,489       <td data-level="2">iPhone</td>
Total net sales     383,285       <th data-level="0">Total net sales</th>

A table whose indented labels all come out at the same level is the failure this rule exists to prevent.

Why flattening is dangerous

The flattened output is well-formed and looks correct. Nothing signals that a parent/child relationship was dropped, so a reader summing the column double-counts: iPhone is inside Total net sales, and the flattened table gives no way to know it. The damage is silent, which is why the indentation MUST be preserved even where the choice of encoding seems secondary.

❌ Counter-sample — 3cc

Structure lost. Under KVO shareholder the page indents two children, Renewable and Nuclear. The rendering below flattens them, leaving a second Renewable with no parent, and it also records 25 for KVO shareholder where the page prints 2.5. The total row is bold across all three cells.

Non-renewable TWh 2.9
KVO shareholder TWh 2.5
Renewable TWh 0.4
Nuclear TWh 2.1
Total energy production TWh 34.8

Reading the level

  • The level MUST be the number of indent steps between the left edge of the stub column and the start of the label as printed. The leftmost label position is 0; each further indent step adds one. A level can therefore be checked against a single row without reading any other.
  • The label text MUST stay verbatim and the rows MUST stay in printed order.
  • Where a table carries levels, every label cell in its stub that prints a label MUST carry one, level-0 rows included. A table whose stub shows no nesting — no indentation, no "of which" rows — and has no labelled total carries none.

Absolute, not relative

A level is read off the print, never inherited from the row above:

  • A row following a level-2 row is level 3 only if the page indents it further. At the same indent it is another level-2 sibling.
  • A row MAY jump back several levels at once. Total net sales returning to 0 after an iPhone at 2 is normal and needs no marker of its own.

Not from the numbers

A level MUST NOT be deepened because the arithmetic suggests a row is a component, and MUST NOT be flattened because the arithmetic does not add up. The indentation is the evidence; the values are not. A page whose sub-items do not sum to their parent is transcribed as printed.

Not as leading whitespace

The level MUST be carried as an attribute, not as leading spaces or  : the first trim, Markdown render or CSV round-trip removes whitespace and the structure goes with it. Where an output format cannot carry a cell attribute, the level SHOULD go into a dedicated level column rather than into whitespace.

Recognising a child row

A child is indented relative to the row above it, and its value is a component of a figure elsewhere in the column rather than an independent record. Phrases such as "out of which", "of which" and "within which" state the same relationship in words; a row introduced by one MUST be rendered as a child even where its indentation is slight. The same page may present a breakdown as an indented stub or as a row that decomposes into sub-rows; both are the same phenomenon and are rendered the same way.

A total row takes a level like any other row, usually 0; how its label cell is marked is defined in Total and Subtotal Rows§9.5.6.

✅ Sample — table-with-breakdown

"- Out of which amount written off" is indented under "Amount involved in frauds": it is a component of that figure, not a peer, so it is level 1. The header labels wrap only for width.

Two more stub shapes

Two-column stubs

Where a table sets sub-labels in a second stub column to the right of the parent label, one per line, each with its own values, the output MUST render a two-column stub: the parent label in the first column, spanning its children with a rowspan where the page prints it as one cell, and each sub-label in the second column on its own row.

✅ Sample — a stub split into two columns

Unallocated interest charges sits in the first stub column, one ruled cell tall enough for both sub-labels, with – external and – intra-group in a second column to its right, each with its own values; the 6 months 2024 cell of – external is empty. Every group on the page closes with an unlabelled bold total. No label is indented, so every label — in either stub column — is level 0; the closing grand total is a labelled total, so its label cell is a <th>.
